body_html:
Spanish gender mistakes are among the first errors learners make, and among the last to disappear. English nouns have no grammatical gender, so the idea that a table is feminine (la mesa) and a book masculine (el libro) feels arbitrary. The good news: most nouns follow clear patterns, and the exceptions that cause trouble are a short, learnable list. Here are the mistakes I see most often, and how to fix them for good.

Key takeaways
  • Most nouns ending in -o are masculine and most ending in -a are feminine, but not all.
  • Words from Greek ending in -ma are usually masculine: el problema, el tema, el idioma.
  • Endings like -ción, -dad, -tud are feminine; -aje and -or are usually masculine.
  • Learn every noun with its article: not mano, but la mano.
{{toc}}

The basic pattern

EndingUsuallyExamples
-omasculineel libro, el perro, el vaso
-afemininela casa, la mesa, la playa
-ción, -siónfemininela canción, la decisión
-dad, -tad, -tudfemininela ciudad, la libertad, la actitud
-umbre, -iefemininela costumbre, la serie
-aje, -ormasculineel viaje, el amor, el color
-ma (Greek origin)masculineel problema, el sistema

The RAE’s Diccionario panhispánico de dudas covers gender in detail, including the many exceptions below.

Spanish gender mistakes with -a and -o words

Masculine words ending in -a

Many of these come from Greek and end in -ma, -pa or -ta:

  • el día (day), el mapa (map), el sofá (sofa)
  • el problema, el tema, el sistema, el programa, el idioma, el clima, el drama
  • el planeta, el cometa (comet)

So it’s Tengo un problema, never una problema, and Buenos días, because día is masculine.

Feminine words ending in -o

  • la mano (hand): the classic exception.
  • la foto (from la fotografía), la moto (from la motocicleta), la radio.

Shortened words keep the gender of the full word, which explains la foto and la moto.

{{image:2}}

El agua: feminine with el

Feminine nouns that start with a stressed a- or ha- take el in the singular, just to make them easier to say: el agua, el águila, el hacha, el alma, el hambre. They are still feminine, so adjectives stay feminine and the plural goes back to las:

  • el agua fría (not frío)
  • las aguas, las almas
  • Tengo mucha hambre (feminine mucha)

That last example also appears in {{link:muy-vs-mucho|muy vs mucho}}.

Words that change meaning with gender

MasculineFeminine
el capital (money)la capital (capital city)
el cura (priest)la cura (cure)
el orden (order, tidiness)la orden (an order, command)
el corte (cut)la corte (court)
el cometa (comet)la cometa (kite)
el frente (front)la frente (forehead)
{{book:the-mind-lies}}

People and professions

Words ending in -ista and -nte often stay the same and only the article changes: el/la artista, el/la turista, el/la estudiante, el/la cantante. Others take a feminine form: el profesor / la profesora, el doctor / la doctora. And a few nouns have one gender no matter who they describe: Juan es una persona muy amable (feminine una persona, even for a man), Ana es un ángel.

Agreement: the mistake after the mistake

Getting the noun right is only half the job. Articles, adjectives and pronouns must agree with it:

  • La casa es blanca. (not blanco)
  • El problema es serio. (not seria)
  • ¿La foto? Ya la vi. (feminine pronoun la)

Common mistakes

IncorrectCorrectWhy

Buenas díasBuenos díasDía is masculine
un persona simpáticouna persona simpáticaPersona is always feminine

{{image:3}}

A few more traps worth knowing

  • el arte is masculine in the singular, but las artes is feminine in the plural: las bellas artes.
  • el mar is usually masculine, but poets and sailors often say la mar.
  • la gente is feminine and singular: La gente es muy amable, never son.
  • el calor and el color are masculine; in some rural areas you may hear la calor, but avoid it.

None of these will stop a conversation, but getting them right is a quiet signal that you have read a lot of Spanish.

How to stop guessing

Always learn nouns with their article: write el mapa in your notes, never just mapa. Color-code flashcards if it helps. And read: after seeing el problema a few hundred times in books, la problema will simply sound wrong. Reading bilingual texts is a great shortcut; I explain why in {{link:parallel-text-reading|parallel text reading}}. For the other big mistake families, see {{link:common-spanish-mistakes|my guide to common Spanish mistakes}}.

{{quiz}}

Final thoughts

Spanish gender isn’t random. Learn the ending patterns, memorize the handful of famous exceptions (el día, el mapa, el problema, la mano, la foto), remember that el agua is feminine, and always make your adjectives agree. Native speakers will forgive the occasional slip, but these fixes will make your Spanish sound much more polished.

faq.q: Why is it el problema and not la problema?
faq.a: Problema comes from Greek, and most Greek-origin words ending in -ma are masculine in Spanish: el problema, el tema, el sistema, el idioma.
Agua is feminine. It takes el in the singular because it starts with a stressed a, but adjectives stay feminine: el agua fría, las aguas.

faq.q: How can I remember the gender of Spanish nouns?
faq.a: Learn each noun with its article, learn the ending patterns (-ción and -dad are feminine, -aje and -or masculine) and memorize the common exceptions.

questions.explain: Greek -ma words are masculine: el problema.
Agua is feminine, so the adjective is fría.
La capital is the city; el capital is money.
